title: The last days, alone
hook: read the last chapter of DN 16
tomorrow: a young man bows to six directions every morning. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sermon: two extremes, a middle way, four truths, and the wheel set rolling. Today, the other end of the road.
screen: `THE WHEEL.` → `THE OTHER END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The last day of a class with a teacher you'll miss has its own quiet. The bell is about to ring, and everybody waits for the one sentence. DN 16 ends that way, between two trees near Kusinara. The Buddha is dying, and the monks have gathered. Ananda is grieving: soon we'll have no teacher. And what he leaves them with is not a successor, and not a relic. It's a sentence.
screen: `THE LAST DAY OF CLASS.` → `BETWEEN TWO TREES, NEAR KUSINARA.` → `NOT A SUCCESSOR. A SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Today's question: what does a teacher leave behind? First, the Buddha tells Ananda, in paraphrase: don't think you have no teacher. The teaching and the discipline I gave you will be your teacher when I'm gone. Then he asks the monks, three times, if anyone has a doubt left. Silence. And then, in the old Rhys Davids English: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Everything made comes apart; strive on. A neighbor tradition has a farewell that sounds close. Paul, writing to the Christians at Philippi, tells them to keep going in his absence: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." Notice those words, work out your salvation, in both old English versions. That's what they share: a teacher stepping away and handing the work to the students, trusting them to continue without him in the room. And the honest difference: Paul's next line says it is God who works in them. The Buddha's last words put the weight on the students' own diligence, with the teaching as their teacher. Even within Buddhism, Shinran leaned on a power beyond the self. Different roads, each described in its own words.
screen: `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.` · `ANY DOUBTS? SILENCE.` · `PAUL: WORK OUT YOUR OWN SALVATION.` · `TWO FAREWELLS, TWO TURNS.` · then, large: `STRIVE ON.`

segments.voice: Sit in silence, the way the monks did after his question. No technique, no counting. Just stay present and awake, as if someone had asked whether you have a doubt left, and you're listening for the answer.
The last days: DN 16, the Buddha's final journey, ending with the teaching as teacher and one last word: strive on.
Strive on: the teacher goes, and the teaching stays right here in your hands. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1707 COUNTS.` → `THE PALI SOURCES, ALONE · 5 OF 12.` → `TOMORROW: SIX DIRECTIONS EVERY MORNING. WHY?`

howItsDone: The Buddha's passing (parinibbana) is remembered on festival days such as Vesak in some traditions and Nirvana Day in others, and his last words are recited and taught as a summary of the path.

Kusinara.meaning: the town where the Buddha died, between two sala trees

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's attendant, at his side at the end

Philippi.meaning: a city in Greece; Paul wrote a letter to its Christians

Shinran.meaning: a Japanese teacher who trusted a power beyond the self

DN 16.meaning: the sutta of the Buddha's last journey and passing

notes: DN 16 chapter 6 paraphrased: Ananda's 'the word of the Teacher is ended, we have no teacher'; the Buddha: the Dhamma and Vinaya will be your teacher; asking the monks three times whether any doubt remains; silence; the last words. Quoted in Rhys Davids's SBE XI (1881) wording: 'Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!' Confirm the exact text and section number (6.10 in some numberings).

Unity thread (wisdom day): shared, a teacher facing absence hands the work to the students (Philippians 2:12, KJV, quoted; 'in my absence' is in the same verse); difference, Philippians 2:13 says God works in them (paraphrased), while DN 16's last word points to the students' diligence with the teaching as teacher. The script adds that within Buddhism Shinran (day 1693) relied on other power, so the difference isn't framed as Buddhism vs. Christianity. Keeper (and a Christian reader) to confirm fairness.
The shared English phrase is an observation about the two old translations, not a claim about why Rhys Davids chose it.
'Between two trees near Kusinara': the twin sala trees; confirm.
